memory_candidates.content: When a .gitignore rule is added to a repo after files matching that pattern are already tracked, git continues to track those pre-existing files (git check-ignore reports them as 'not ignored' due to the tracked-file exception). Before assuming a gitignored pattern makes files git-unrecoverable in a cleanup/deletion task, run `git ls-files <pattern>` to check whether some of those files are actually still tracked -- the real git-recoverability margin may be wider than a size/count estimate based on the .gitignore rule alone.

For irreversible/destructive cross-repo cleanup tasks (deleting large gitignored data outside the working repo), the safe pattern is: (1) record a full sha256 manifest and re-verify equivalence against the surviving source-of-truth immediately before any destructive action -- treat ANY mismatch or missing file as a hard abort, not a partial success; (2) create a backup and independently re-hash it against the pre-delete manifest before deleting anything; (3) delete only the exact target path; (4) re-run any read-only regression check (e.g. a briefing/resolution script) before and after, diffing the two outputs for byte-identical output as the zero-cost check; (5) commit the tracked-file deletion locally only, never push/PR from an automated agent.
